headline: The Pelicans have a young identity, navy and gold with a fleur-de-lis pelican, and a fanbase that wants the city's real second-line and Mardi Gras Indian color on the jersey instead of a tourist-guide version.
summary: The Pelicans launched in 2013 with a navy, gold and red palette and a pelican-with-fleur-de-lis mark, replacing the Hornets' teal and purple, which stayed with Charlotte. The 2023-24 'NOLA Nights' City Edition (purple with neon green and a skeletal 'Skelican' mark, a night-streets concept rather than a Mardi Gras one) was loved enough that the 2025-26 City Edition brought it back. The brand has no deep classic era of its own, so New Orleans-made merch (Saints-adjacent Who Dat culture, second-line style, local screen-printers) fills the gap. The opening is real local storytelling, built with the people who own those traditions, on a team entering 2026-27 with low expectations, a new coach (Jamahl Mosley) and a 26-56 season behind it.

insights.title: Young identity, no deep classic era
insights.detail: The Pelicans brand dates to 2013 and the franchise's 2002-13 Hornets history sits with Charlotte, so there is no multi-decade throwback vault to mine. Fans' emotional anchors are Anthony Davis, Chris Paul-era Hornets memories, and Zion.
insights.implication: Classic Edition is a weak lever here. Nike should put its design energy into City Edition and lifestyle product built from the city, not the franchise archive.

insights.title: A returning City Edition shows what fans want
insights.detail: The 2025-26 City Edition reissued the 2023-24 design, which fans had singled out as a favorite. A team repeating a City Edition signals unusually strong demand for one look.
insights.implication: Study what made the 2023-24 design land before briefing a 2026-27 concept, and avoid replacing it with something more generic. Verify the 2026-27 City Edition status first.

insights.title: Mardi Gras purple, green and gold is expected but flattened
insights.detail: Carnival purple, green and gold is the city's default shorthand (the 2023-24 'Skelican' edition used purple and neon green but as a night-life look). Locals read Carnival color as a given, so fans respond more to specifics: krewe culture, the Zulu and Rex traditions, and the neighborhood second-line clubs.
insights.implication: Move from the generic three-color stripe to named, credited local references, with purple, green and gold used with restraint against navy.

insights.title: Real merch lives in New Orleans culture, not team shops
insights.detail: Local screen-printed shirts, Who Dat-style vernacular, Saints and Pelicans crossovers and neighborhood-pride tees (Seventh Ward, Ninth Ward, Westbank, Uptown) move more than generic team gear. Fans trade on area codes, wards and slang.
insights.implication: Collaborate with local New Orleans printers and designers, and build neighborhood-first graphics that the team's own shop does not.

insights.title: Mardi Gras Indian and second-line craft is the biggest untouched design language
insights.detail: Black Masking Indian suits, hand-sewn beadwork and feather work, and brass-band second-line parades from the Tremé and Seventh Ward are the city's most distinctive visual tradition. They are sacred and living, not decoration.
insights.implication: Treat this as a partnership, credit and pay the tribes' and artists' communities, and borrow the logic (color layering, patchwork, hand-stitched texture) rather than lifting suit imagery.

insights.title: Zion and Murphy are the faces, but the team is rebuilding fan trust
insights.detail: After two sub-30-win seasons, a 26-56 record and a coaching change to Jamahl Mosley, fan sentiment is cautious. Zion Williamson remains the marquee jersey, with Trey Murphy III, Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears as the younger faces.
insights.implication: Lean on player product (Zion, Murphy) and on city pride rather than team-performance narratives, and keep launch volume measured.

places.name: Smoothie King Center
places.why: The Pelicans' home arena, adjacent to the Superdome, where the city's pro-sports merch culture meets Who Dat Saints culture.

places.name: Louis Armstrong Park and Congo Square
places.why: The historic gathering site of African and Afro-Caribbean music and dance, and the cultural root of second-line and Black New Orleans music.

places.name: Backstreet Cultural Museum
places.why: Long-running museum of Mardi Gras Indian suits, social aid and pleasure club regalia and jazz funeral tradition, and a respected partner point for any cultural work.

places.name: Magazine Street
places.why: Local boutique and streetwear retail spine where New Orleans-made brands sell.

places.name: Dooky Chase's Restaurant
places.why: A landmark of Creole cooking and Black civil rights history, representative of the heritage layer fans treat as the city's own.

places.name: Xavier University of Louisiana
places.why: A historically Black university with a strong local sports and style culture, and a youth-facing partner.

people.name: Zion Williamson
people.why: The franchise's biggest jersey draw and the most visible face of the team.

people.name: Trey Murphy III
people.why: Breakout scorer at 21.5 points per game last season, and a rising second player face for product.

people.name: Derik Queen
people.why: Young big man acquired in the trade that cost the team its 2026 first-round pick.

people.name: Jeremiah Fears
people.why: Young guard in the team's new core.

people.name: Jamahl Mosley
people.why: New head coach in 2026-27 who replaced Willie Green.

people.name: Anthony Davis
people.why: The Pelicans-era icon whose number and unibrow-era jerseys fans still wear.

people.name: Trombone Shorty
people.why: A Tremé-born brass musician and ambassador of New Orleans' musical culture whose imagery is widely recognized.

people.name: Big Freedia
people.why: The best-known face of bounce music, a distinct local sound for neighborhood-first collaborations.

moments.name: Carnival season and Mardi Gras
moments.why: The city's biggest color moment, and the obvious but easy window for purple, green and gold product.

moments.name: Super Sunday and St. Joseph's Night
moments.why: The Mardi Gras Indian tribes' public gatherings, a moment for respectful, credited partnership, not product drops.

moments.name: New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival
moments.why: The city's major music festival and a spring, non-NBA moment for local culture.

moments.name: Southern Decadence and Essence Festival
moments.why: Essence Festival of Culture draws a large Black audience to the Superdome and Smoothie King Center area.

moments.name: NBA Cup group play
moments.why: Pelicans are in West Group B with OKC, MIN, LAC and MEM, with a Cup opener at the Clippers on Oct 30.

moments.name: Season opener
moments.why: The 2026-27 home opener is the first chance to show a new uniform set and the Mosley era.

moments.name: Saints season
moments.why: The football season dominates local sports attention in the fall, so cross-sport crossover product competes for the same fans.

designCues.cue: Pelicans navy as the base, with Carnival gold used as a thin accent
designCues.use: Keep navy dominant so the team stays recognizable, and use Carnival colors as accents instead of full-body purple.

designCues.cue: Old gold, a muted gold that reads as brass rather than yellow
designCues.source: Official Pelicans gold, echoing brass instruments and wrought iron
designCues.use: Use for trim, numerals and metal-look hardware on product.

designCues.cue: Carnival purple as a restrained secondary
designCues.source: Mardi Gras color tradition (purple for justice)
designCues.use: Apply as a gradient or lining color, and avoid a full striped Carnival set.

designCues.cue: Wrought-iron balcony lacework as a line pattern
designCues.source: French Quarter and Garden District ironwork
designCues.use: Tone-on-tone tonal graphic on warm-ups and hoodies, drawn as a custom pattern, not a photo.

designCues.source: Second-line club regalia and social aid and pleasure club style
designCues.use: Reference layered fabric and trim in a collaboration with a local designer, never copying specific club or tribe designs.

designCues.source: Corner stores, po-boy shops and neighborhood signs
designCues.use: A custom neighborhood-name wordmark for tees and hats, drawn by a New Orleans lettering artist.

designCues.cue: Fleur-de-lis reduced to a clean modern mark
designCues.source: City and state heraldry, already part of the Pelicans logo
designCues.use: Use sparingly, since the Saints and city also own this symbol, and avoid the stock clip-art version.

designCues.source: Local neighborhood identity, including the 504 area code
designCues.use: Build neighborhood tees with local artists and credit them.

productHooks: A neighborhood capsule (Seventh Ward, Tremé, Central City, Ninth Ward, Westbank) designed with New Orleans artists, sold at Magazine Street shops and online.
A Zion and Trey Murphy III player pack with ironwork-pattern graphics and navy and old gold colorways.
A Carnival-season warm-up and shooting shirt that uses purple only as a lining, released ahead of Mardi Gras.
A bounce and brass-band collaboration capsule with a local artist, with royalties to the artist and a music-education partner.
A hat and jacket line using hand-painted shop-sign lettering for neighborhood names.
watchouts: Mardi Gras Indian suits, Black Masking Indian imagery and feather or bead designs are sacred, community-owned work. Do not copy them. Partner, credit and pay if engaging at all.
Who Dat and fleur-de-lis marks carry Saints and city licensing history, so check IP before using them.
Avoid tourist shorthand (Bourbon Street, voodoo, 'Nawlins') and hurricane-trauma imagery.
Do not reference or imitate specific krewes' or second-line clubs' regalia without their consent.
Do not rely on past City Edition detail in this file without checking, since concepts and years are from memory.

eras.look: Navy, gold and red with a pelican and fleur-de-lis primary logo and a custom wordmark.
eras.legacy: The franchise's only identity as the Pelicans, tied to Anthony Davis and Zion Williamson.

eras.look: Teal, purple and gold with the Hugo hornet mark.
eras.legacy: Remembered fondly in the city, though the team history now sits with Charlotte, so New Orleans fans can't wear it as an official throwback.

cityEditions.concept: A reissue of the 2023-24 'NOLA Nights' / 'Skelican' City Edition design.
cityEditions.note: The return signals strong demand for the 2023-24 look. Verify the 2026-27 City Edition.

cityEditions.concept: 'NOLA Nights': vivid purple with neon green accents, skeletonized logos and a custom NOLA wordmark, inspired by the city's streets and lights at night.
cityEditions.note: Cited as a fan favorite, as shown by its 2025-26 return.

cityEditions.concept: Concepts for the other seasons (2017-18 to 2022-23, 2024-25) were not verified; the 2024-25 edition exists but its design was not checked.
cityEditions.note: Per-season concepts and reception need a live check.

untoldStories.story: The Seventh Ward and Tremé social aid and pleasure club second-line tradition, told with club permission.
untoldStories.why: It is the city's own parade culture and not a tourist symbol, and a jersey story should come from the community.

untoldStories.story: Congo Square and the roots of New Orleans' music, from brass bands to bounce.
untoldStories.why: It ties the city's identity to a place and gives a deeper story than Mardi Gras color alone.

untoldStories.story: The levee-and-Gulf identity of the Ninth Ward and the West Bank, including post-Katrina rebuilding told by residents.
untoldStories.why: It gives neighborhoods outside the French Quarter a place on the product, if handled with care and local voices.

untoldStories.story: The Hornets-to-Pelicans transition and the 2005 return after Hurricane Katrina.
untoldStories.why: It is a lived franchise chapter that few fans see in product, though it needs sensitivity.
